name: Ribeye and water carnivore

card.summary: Strict carnivore eating built around fatty steak and water: a monotony-based protocol with no studies of its own.
card.note: Not described as a distinct named protocol in the sources; evidence applies only to the broader carnivore diet.

quick.overview:
Ribeye and water describes a very strict form of carnivore eating in which fatty steak is the main or only food. Grokipedia does not treat it as a separate named protocol, but notes carnivore advocates recommend fatty cuts such as ribeye, 80/20 ground beef and added tallow so that most calories come from fat.

Supporters describe simplicity and symptom relief. No study has tested it specifically.
quick.mechanism: Fat and protein supply energy with near-zero carbohydrate, typically in ketosis. Fatty cuts are favoured to avoid protein-heavy eating.
quick.risks: Concerns about the wider carnivore diet include fibre and micronutrient gaps, a documented scurvy case with mostly canned beef, raised LDL cholesterol, constipation, gout and kidney strain.

lead: Ribeye and water is a shorthand for an extremely narrow carnivore diet built around fatty beef steaks and water. Grokipedia does not describe it as a distinct named protocol, but notes that carnivore advocates recommend fatty cuts such as ribeye, 80/20 ground beef and added tallow so that most calories come from fat rather than protein.[2]

It belongs to the carnivore diet family, which allows only animal foods and excludes plants.[1] Evidence for the family consists mainly of self-reports; dietetic bodies classify the diet as a fad diet.[1][2]
infobox: Shawn Baker, Mikhaila and Jordan Peterson

paras: Carnivore advocates favour fatty cuts of ruminant meat to supply most energy as fat, since very lean meat without enough fat can cause fatigue, nausea and diarrhoea, a condition Grokipedia calls protein poisoning or rabbit starvation.[2] The ribeye-and-water pattern reduces variety to a minimum, which proponents present as a simple elimination approach.

The wider carnivore diet was promoted from 2018 by Shawn Baker, and Mikhaila and Jordan Peterson followed an even stricter beef, salt and water version.[1] Historical precedents include Salisbury's 1880s lean-beef regimen and Vilhjalmur Stefansson's 1928 supervised meat-only year.[1][2]

Wikipedia lists missing fibre, vitamin deficiencies, raised LDL cholesterol, constipation, and colon cancer and gout risk with high red-meat intake as concerns; the British Dietetic Association and Dietitians Australia classify the diet as a fad.[1] Grokipedia adds scurvy, kidney-stone and bone concerns and notes that health bodies generally advise against long-term adherence.[2]
No studies found. A 2021 survey of carnivore dieters reported high self-rated improvement, but it was self-selected and did not test a ribeye-only pattern.[2]
